projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Irvin Gaynor was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay to get started, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And what were some of the reasons you enlisted for?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I enlisted because I was patriotic, and I enlisted at the age of seventeen, and that was before I finished high school. That was my senior year, because I thought that if I enlisted I would be able to get some benefits and breaks other than going into the infantry. I was able to choose my branch of service.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay and where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: In Chicago, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Why did you pick the US Army Medical Corps?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I picked that because I was interested in [medicine], and I wanted to go to medical school, and that was really the primary reason.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What did you want to do in medicine?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I wanted to be a doctor, but at that time I had no specific specialties that I was really interested in pursuing.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, do you recall your first day or first few days in the service?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I sure do!

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Can you describe that?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, I went into the service wearing civilian clothes. I went to Camp Grant, Illinois, which is near Peoria, Illinois and I was then issued my GI clothing and my GJ shoes and all of that. I went to my barracks, and I realized that I was no longer a civilian, I was now a soldier.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And what emotions did that evoke? What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, I mean it just was a hard feeling to describe. It was the beginning of a different phase of life. I was no longer a civilian and no longer living at home. I had never been away from home prior to that.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And when was that? What year did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: What year? I believe that was 1943.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So the war had already started?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes, the war started in 1941.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What kind oftraining or camp did you have to go through to get ready?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: When I went into service?

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I took my basic training. Actually, it was infantry basic training.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And what did that involve?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: That involved obstacle courses, learning how to handle a rifle, a machine gun, a .45 caliber handgun and a bayonet, and just infantry training.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was that difficult to get through?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Extremely. For me it was extremely difficult to handle.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was it just due to physical reasons?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Physical aspects of the [training] were very very difficult. Climbing walls, jumping into trenches. There was always artificial gunfire which sounded exactly like real gunfire. We had to hunker down. It was very difficult, very strenuous. Both physically and emotionally.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay and now during and after your training where did you go during the war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: We stayed at Camp Grant and then I was sent back to Chicago. I was given something, I don't know what it is called, like a furlough, and I was placed in the Army Specialized Training Program, ASTP. They let me go to the University of Illinois in Champaign to complete part of my college education. After that I went back to Chicago still as part of the Anny Specialized Training Program, and as a soldier, I went to dental school at the University of Illinois.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So you stayed in Illinois your whole time?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: All the time that I was in the service. And for that I had to stay in the reserves indefinitelyyin the army reserves.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Do you remember arriving at all the different places?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Do I remember? Of course!

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Nothing spectacular. It was just going from place to place and knowing that there was a war going on and that I really wasn't a part of it because of my education and really luck. Also, that I never knew when I would have to go overseas. But at no time did I have to go.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Were you happy that you were able to get an education during the war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes. Very. There were very few of us that were able to do that and I felt extremely fortunate and blessed by the opportunity.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you ever see combat?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, since I never went overseas.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Or did you ever have any injuries due to camp or any other reasons?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: While I was at Camp Grant I did guard duty many times over the German prisoners of war. And I got to talk to some of them, because at that time I was able to speak German fluently, because I took a lot of German in college.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And no injuries during camp?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Most memorable? Well, the most memorable was when the war ended in [1945]. While at that time I was still a junior in dental school I think, and the most memorable was the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What was that like for everyone and yourself. What was going through your mind during that day?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, just that the war was over and we were victorious over the Germans. A year later we were then victorious over the Japanese. I felt like now I could go on living my life again. As I told you earlier, I stayed in the reserves and during the Korean War that broke out in 1950, I was still there in the reserves. At that time, I was called back into active duty. I did not have to go to Korea or anything of that nature and during that period, I obtained the rank of major. Some time between 1950 and oh, I don't know, around 1952 or '53 or something and I stayed in the reserves until about 1960 I would guess when I was discharged with the rank of lieutenant colonel.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: When the war ended what was more significant to you? The Germans or the Japanese surrendering?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh both. Of course you know the GenTIans were a very vicious aImy when they killed so many people. I had no empathy for either the Germans or the Japanese. It was a great victory and we put down fascism so that democracy could triumph.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was there excitement when the Germans surrendered? Even though you were still fighting in the war with Japan?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Excitement! Oh yes, it was pandemonium. There was so much excitement. It was the beginning of a new era.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Even though the war was still going on with Japan?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah see, the Japanese war ended when we dropped an atom bomb on Hiroshima. Then three days later we dropped one on the city of Nagasaki. That caused the Japanese to soon repeat, and that's how the war ended there. If we had not, we probably would have had to invade Japan with the resulting loss of thousands and thousands of American troops.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Even though the United states was done fighting with Germany, people were still nervous about Japan?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah, we were still, of course, fighting Japan in the south Pacific. I think if we had not have dropped the bombs we would have to had invaded Japan. So that's controversial. Some people feel like we shouldn't have done that, but I think it was the right decision by President Harry Truman.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, so you thought it would have taken a longer time to handle if we had not dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes, I thought it was the correct decision.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, I have a couple of medals. I don't even really remember what they are. World War 2 service. Good conduct metals. I don't know, I have about three, four, five or six medals. I don't even remember what they were all for.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So do you remember any specific reasons for having gotten them?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, not having been in combat, these were just medals that the Army gives you for length of service and stuff of that nature. I was never in combat, so thank God I don't have a purple heart or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, during the service what were some of the ways you stayed in touch with friends and family?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, I stayed in touch primarily by writing. You know we didn't have computers and email then. Yeah, I stayed in touch by writing letters.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was that difficult to do because you were living in Illinois?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, not at all, it was really good. It was good therapy.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: When you were in camp what was the food like?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: It wasn't bad, it was typical army food but it was good. It was nutritious. It was not bad.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies, because so much was going overseas?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh yes. There were no shortages for us.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was there something you did for good luck in camp or school?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Good luck? No, not really.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well they had the USOs where we could go and dance with local girls. There was no shortage of entertainment for the troops who were stationed in the United States.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What did you do when you were on leave from service?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, usually go to USOs and we went to movies. Mainly dances and stuff of that nature.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How long and how often were you usually on leave?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Usually we would get a two or three day pass.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How often?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I'd say every three months if I can remember correctly.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you travel anywhere when you were in service?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah, different places in the United States. The states of Washington, Oregon, California, South Carolina, and Georgia. 18:15I

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And was that army-related?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So what did you do when you were there?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: It was all part of the training program. Different programs.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Do you recall any funny or unusual events that occurred?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, I don't.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: And did you pull pranks on other people?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Do you have any photographs from the war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Who's in them and where are they?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: They are in the house, but there are many photographs.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Where were they usually taken?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: At the various camps that I was at.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Were they with fellow members ofthe army?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: They're all just pictures of me in my uniform, with different soldiers and stuff of that nature.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, what did you think ofthe people you worked with?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I thought they were excellent and very high caliber.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you ever keep a diary?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Not offhand, no. I don't recall the specific day, no.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: But do you remember what happened that day?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, I remember that I was discharged at the convenience of the army.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How did you find out?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: My commanding officer informed me.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Where were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I was then in dental school in Chicago.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What did you do in the upcoming days and weeks?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, nothing. I continued to go to school. It was no holiday or anything.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did it feel any different when you went [to school]?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah, you went from wearing a uniform to becoming a civilian again.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So you stayed in school. Did you work?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, not at the time.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Was your education supported by the GI bill?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you have any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Many, yes.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Are you still in touch with any of them?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Absolutely. When I was in dental school I made many close friends, but most of them are no longer living or in nursing homes. So I'm one of the fortunate ones so far.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you meet any of those friends during training?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh yes, certainly.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you join a Veterans Organization?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes, I was in the American Legion.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What did you go on to do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: After the war, I became a dentist. That is what I am still doing.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: At what point did you decide that you wanted to become a dentist?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, it was really a decision that the army made for me. After my training they offered me the opportunity to go to dental school. That's how I made the decision.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did they offer you any other fields of medicine?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, that was the only option available to me at the time. It was either that I go to dental school, or that I go overseas as a medic. I chose to go to dental school.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: When you knew you wanted to be a doctor, was that one of your choices?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Well, I really would have preferred to be a medical doctor but I didn't have that option at the time.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So do you regret becoming a dentist?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, no. I like being a dentist.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thoughts about war and the military in general?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Perhaps so, but I'm not certain.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did the service have a positive or negative effect?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I'd say neutral. Neither negative or positive.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, what kinds of activities does your veterans association do?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, well, they just supported veterans who were injured in combat and visited VA hospitals and widows of soldiers who were killed.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: What did you do with them?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I just really visited wounded veterans in hospitals who had been treated and were being brought back to civilian life.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Did you attend reunions of the military?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How did the experience of service affect your life?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Wow, that's a big question. It matured me rapidly. I grew up quickly. I came to realize that war is just a horrible thing. It disrupts everything and everybody's life.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So it contributed to your dislike of war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Oh, I dislike war very much.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Is that solely because of what you went through during war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: It's really because it's just bad for people. There's no value in war.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Can you elaborate on some of your experiences during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I was just stationed in Texas. At that time I was already a dentist, and so all I did during that period was dentistry for army personnel.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How did you get promoted to different ranks?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I guess because I did my job well. The officers above me gave me promotions, because I did whatever I was told to do and did it well.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: How often were you promoted?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I was promoted usually in two year intervals, I would say.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Once you were recalled, how long did you serve?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: I served for two or two-and-a-half more years.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: So you spent that whole time in Texas?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yes

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: After that where did you continue to do dentistry?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: In Texas.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Are there any important events that you were involved in during the war?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: No, I think that about covers it.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: If possible, can I follow up with post-interview questions later on?

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Yeah, definitely if you need to.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay thank you so much for taking the time to do the interview.

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, thank you. I really enjoyed the interview. The questions were clear and concise and really brought back memories. It was really an excellent interview.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Thank you so much.

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: Don't hesitate to ask anymore questions as needed.

sp.speaker: Adam Gaynor
sp.p: Okay, thank you again.

sp.speaker: Irvin Gaynor
sp.p: You're very welcome.
